hook.text: Archaeology isn't about treasure hunting. It's about reading the stories that broken pots and buried bones tell.

buildup.text: Archaeology studies past human societies through their material remains — artifacts, structures, and landscapes.

discovery.text: It fills gaps that written history can't. Most human cultures left no texts, only objects buried in the ground.

twist.text: Archaeology reveals ordinary lives, not just kings and wars. A trash pit tells more than a monument sometimes.

climax.text: Through objects, archaeology reconstructs how people lived, ate, traded, worshipped, and died across millennia.

punchline.text: The past speaks through what it left behind.

quiz.question: What does archaeology study?
options: Past societies through their material remains

details.summary: Archaeology studies past human societies through their material remains — artifacts, structures, landscapes, and biological evidence. Unlike history, which relies on written records, archaeology can investigate the 99% of human existence that predates writing.
details.whyItMatters: Archaeology gives voice to the voiceless past. Most humans who ever lived left no written records. Without archaeology, the vast majority of human experience — and the lessons it holds — would be permanently inaccessible.
takeaways: Archaeology studies the past through material remains, not texts
It accesses the 99% of human history that predates writing
Material evidence reveals what written records cannot capture

faq.question: How does archaeology differ from history?
faq.answer: History relies on written documents and is limited to literate societies from roughly 5,000 years ago. Archaeology uses physical evidence and can investigate millions of years of human and pre-human activity. Even in historical periods, archaeology reveals what documents omit.

faq.question: Is archaeology only about digging up old things?
faq.answer: No. Modern archaeology includes laboratory analysis, remote sensing, digital modeling, and ethnographic study of living communities. Excavation is just one method. Interpreting what material remains mean about past human lives is the core intellectual challenge.
